opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What excites me most is that, for a long time, building safety systems meant training a separate, narrow classifier for every individual risk. You'd need a big labeled dataset for hate speech, another for self-harm, another for violence, and each one was expensive, slow to build, and brittle. When a new risk came along or the context changed, you were essentially starting over.

Generative models change that equation. The same capabilities that make them powerful for building applications, like understanding nuance, following instructions, and reasoning about context, make them powerful for building defenses. We can describe a policy in natural language and have a model help evaluate content against it. We can use models to generate adversarial test data, simulating the kinds of attacks or misuse we're worried about, at a scale and variety human red teamers alone could never reach. And we can build detectors for brand-new problems like jailbreaks, prompt injection, or ungrounded outputs much faster than before.

There's also a nice symmetry: the technology introducing new risks is also giving us better tools to manage them. That means safety can keep pace with innovation instead of always lagging behind. It's not a silver bullet. You still need humans in the loop, careful measurement, and layered defenses, because models used as judges have their own failure modes. But it dramatically lowers the cost and raises the speed of building safety into systems, and that means more teams can actually do it well, not just the largest organizations with huge specialized budgets.

r001.rationale: The response mentions that context can change, but does not state that the same statement may be hateful in one context and not hateful in another.

r002.rationale: It describes generating adversarial test data to simulate attacks and misuse, but does not say generative models produce harmful content as synthetic training data for safety models.

r003.rationale: It says models understand nuance and reason about context, and that these capabilities make them powerful for building defenses and detectors.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, it's great to be here. So, I've been working in responsible AI at Microsoft for a long time now, and for most of that time, safety work has been really hard and really manual. If you wanted to detect harmful content, you had to go collect a labeled dataset, train a classifier, and then the moment the kind of content you cared about shifted a little, you were back to square one. It didn't generalize well, and it was slow.

What's exciting to me about generative AI is that, for the first time, the same capability that creates the risk also gives us a much more powerful tool for managing it. These models understand language and context in a way that earlier classifiers just didn't. So I can take a policy that a human wrote in plain English, something like "we don't want the system giving medical advice," and I can have a model reason about whether a given output violates that policy. I don't need thousands of labeled examples up front. I can iterate on the policy itself, test it, refine it, and deploy it in days instead of months.

The other piece is that we can now use these models to find problems before customers do. Red teaming used to be a small group of people sitting in a room trying to break the system by hand. Now we can use generative AI to automate a lot of that, generate adversarial prompts at scale, cover many more harm categories and many more languages, and then surface the interesting failures for humans to look at. That dramatically changes how much ground we can cover.

And then on the evaluation side, we can use models as judges to measure things like groundedness or whether a response is actually relevant to the question, and do that continuously rather than just once before launch. So you end up with this whole loop: measure, mitigate, measure again, and the generative models are helping at every stage.

I want to be clear that it's not magic. These safety models have their own failure modes, and we still absolutely need humans in the loop and traditional techniques alongside them. But the velocity at which we can build and improve safety systems is just fundamentally different than it was even two years ago, and that's what gets me excited.

r001.rationale: The response mentions language and context generally, but does not state that the same statement can be hateful in one context and not hateful in another.

r002.rationale: It describes generating adversarial prompts for red teaming, but does not identify harmful-content generation as a source of synthetic training data for safety models.

r003.rationale: It says generative models understand language and context better than earlier classifiers and uses that ability to assess policy violations.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that generative AI gives us new tools for building the safety systems themselves. A lot of safety challenges depend on context: the same words can mean very different things depending on what someone is asking and why. Models that can work with that context give us an opportunity to build more nuanced protections.

They can also help us explore ways a system might fail, generate examples to test against, and help people review potential problems. You still need to evaluate those tools carefully—they can make mistakes too—but there’s a really promising opportunity to use advances in AI to make AI safer.

r003.rationale: It links contextual understanding and nuance to building safety systems, but does not identify safety classifiers as the target.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that generative AI gives us a much more flexible way to understand context. Safety isn’t just about spotting a particular word or matching a pattern. The same language can mean very different things depending on what someone is asking, why they’re asking it, and how the system responds.

We can use these models to help evaluate those interactions and build safeguards that handle more nuanced situations. They can also help us test systems—generating challenging examples, exploring potential failure modes, and helping us find gaps before users encounter them.

Of course, those safety systems need to be evaluated carefully, too. But there’s a really exciting opportunity here: as the models become more capable, we can use those capabilities to improve the tools we have for making AI safer.

r003.rationale: It describes generative AI as better at understanding context and says that contextual flexibility helps build safeguards for nuanced situations.
